Money, Work and Pay.text: Yen pays for everything, and most people earn it the ordinary way: salaried office jobs, shifts in shops and restaurants, deliveries, factories and building sites. A part-time job pays roughly 1,000 to 1,300 yen an hour, settled on payday; a convenience-store snack costs a few hundred yen, a restaurant meal 500 to 1,500, a local train ride a few hundred, and a month's rent for a small city apartment tens of thousands. U.A. students live in Heights Alliance and pay for what they buy outside it (cafeteria meals, food, phones, clothes, weekends in town) from family money or a part-time job. Pro heroes are paid a public-service fee for each case they resolve, on top of their agency's income from merchandise, endorsements and appearances, which is why case credit is money; sidekicks draw salaries from the agency. Police officers and teachers are salaried public servants. Villains live on cash jobs paid through brokers, stolen goods sold to fences and debts owed to people who collect. Once a price, a wage or a debt is named it stays fixed, and nobody is paid for attending a lesson or for doing the right thing.
